title: The Lighthouse · 10
paragraphs: So this was the island, Cam thought, as she trailed her fingers through the waves again. Never before had she seen it from out at sea. So that was how it lay on the water: a dent in its middle, two sharp crags, the sea sweeping in there and stretching away for mile after mile on either side. It was tiny—shaped rather like a leaf standing on its end. So we took a little boat, she thought, and began telling herself an adventure story about escaping from a ship that was going down. But with the sea running through her fingers, and a sprig of seaweed disappearing behind them, she had no wish to tell herself a story in earnest. What she wanted was the feeling of adventure and escape. For as the boat sailed on she was thinking how everything had slipped away, passed, streamed off behind them: her father’s fury over the points of the compass, James’s obstinacy about their compact, her own misery. So what came next? Where were they heading? Out of her hand, icy cold, sunk deep in the sea, a fountain of joy shot up—joy at the change, the escape, the adventure (that she was alive, that she was here). And the drops from this sudden, thoughtless fountain fell here and there on the dark, drowsing shapes in her mind—shapes of a world she had not yet made real, turning in their darkness and catching a spark of light here and there: Greece, Rome, Constantinople. Tiny as it was, like a leaf on end, with the gold-flecked water flowing in and around it, did even that little island, she wondered, have its place in the universe? The old gentlemen in the study could have told her, she thought. Now and then she wandered in from the garden on purpose to catch them at it. There they would be (Mr. Carmichael, perhaps, or Mr. Bankes, very old and very stiff), facing each other in their low armchairs, crackling the pages of _The Times_ in front of them. She would come in from the garden with everything muddled in her head: something someone had said about Christ; a mammoth dug up in a London street; what had the great Napoleon been like? And they would take all this up in their clean hands (their clothes were gray; they smelled of heather), brush the scraps together, turn the paper, cross their knees, and every so often say something very short. As if in a trance, she would take a book off the shelf and stand watching her father write—so evenly, so neatly, from one edge of the page across to the other—coughing a little now and then, or saying something brief to the other old gentleman across from him. And standing there with her book open, she thought: here you could let any thought you had unfold like a leaf in water; and if it did well here, among the smoking old gentlemen and the crackle of _The Times_, then it was right. And as she watched her father writing in his study, she thought (sitting in the boat now) that he was utterly lovable and utterly wise; he was not vain, and he was no tyrant. Indeed, if he noticed her there with her book, he would ask her, as gently as anyone could, Was there nothing he could give her?

To make sure this was not wrong, she looked at him as he read the little book whose glossy cover was speckled like a plover’s egg. No; it was right. Look at him now, she wanted to say out loud to James. (But James was watching the sail.) He’s a sarcastic brute, James would answer. He always turns the conversation to himself and his books, James would say. His egotism is unbearable. And worst of all, he’s a tyrant. But look! she said, looking at him. Look at him now. She watched him reading, his legs curled up, the little book with the yellowish pages she knew so well without knowing a word of what was on them. It was a small book, in close print. On the flyleaf, she knew, he had noted down fifteen francs spent on dinner; so much for the wine; so much as a tip for the waiter; everything neatly totaled at the foot of the page. But what might be written inside—in a book whose corners had been worn round by his pocket—she had no idea. None of them knew what he thought. Yet he was so absorbed that when he glanced up, as he did now for a moment, it was not to look at anything; it was to pin some thought down more precisely. Once that was done his mind flew back and he dived into his reading again. He read, she thought, like someone steering something, or coaxing a great flock of sheep along, or forcing his way higher and higher up one narrow path. At times he went quickly and straight, breaking through the undergrowth; at times a branch seemed to lash at him, a bramble to blind him—but he would not let that defeat him; on he went, turning over page after page. And she kept telling herself her story about escaping from a sinking ship, for as long as he sat there she was safe—as safe as she felt when she slipped in from the garden and took down a book, and the old gentleman abruptly lowered his paper and said something very short over the top of it about Napoleon’s character.

She looked back across the sea toward the island. But the leaf was growing blurred at the edges. It was so small now, and so far off. The sea counted for more than the shore now. All around them waves were heaving and sinking; a log wallowed down one of them, a gull rode on another. Somewhere near here, she thought, dipping her fingers in the water, a ship had gone down; and dreamily, half asleep, she murmured how we perished, each alone.
